Constitutional Considerations in Agency Reasoning. In unexcerpted 
portions of both the majority and dissenting opinions, the justices disagreed 
about the role of constitutional concerns in agency decision making. Justice 
Scalia’s majority opinion explicitly rejected any invitation “to apply a more 
stringent arbitrary-and-capricious review to agency actions that implicate 
constitutional hberties.” Justice Stevens would have struck down the agency 
action as arbitrary and capricious, in part because he believed that the agency 
had strayed far from the Court’s past interpretations of the types of indecency 
regulation the First Amendment permitted and had “failed to demonstrate an 
awareness” that it had done so. Justice Breyer writing for the four dissenting 
justices simply would have remanded to the agency because the FCC failed to 
address the constitutional “aspect” of the problem. But, as the disposition on 
remand illustrates, the courts will ultimately decide the constitutional 
questions for themselves. For an argument that constitutional concerns and

Administrative Law as Constitutional Common Law, 110 COLUM. L. Re v . 479 
(2010).
5. 
Substance or Process'? Justice Breyer’s dissent characterizes 
arbitrary and capricious review as an examination of the agency’s reasoning 
process in which the court seeks to determine whether the agency has 
considered all of the relevant criteria and excluded irrelevant ones. This 
conventional approach is meant to distance the reviewing court from the 
substantive policy determinations that it is reviewing. Proceduralized 
rationality review in this form is sometimes described as leaving an agency 
free to determine the substantive weight to be assigned to various 
considerations so long as it has effectively considered them all. But, there is 
surely a fine fine between assessing whether an agency has given sufficiently 
good reasons and determining what weight any particular considerations 
should have in its overall analysis. There would be no reason, for example, for 
Justice Breyer to befieve that the FCC’s analysis of the importance of new 
bleeping technology was inadequate unless he thought that the FCC had given 
too httle weight to the difficulties of local broadcasters and the importance of 
local broadcast capacity in the overall scheme of federal communications 
regulation. And reviewing courts are surely motivated to rigorously examine 
an agency’s reasons and to hold it to stricter procedural requirements where 
the agency action simply seems wrong-headed.
6. 
DACA Revisited. In Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of 
the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), the Supreme Court declared 
arbitrary and capricious the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) 
attempted revocation of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) 
program. The opinion for the Court by Chief Justice Roberts was a significant 
apphcation of the Court’s arbitrary-and-capricious precedents in a high-profile 
case.
